title: Puerto Rican-Style Pollo Guisado (Chicken Stew with Potatoes and Carrots)
description: Chicken thighs braised with sofrito, tomato sauce, potatoes, and carrots until the sauce turns thick and savory. Two pounds of thighs feed six over rice, at roughly $2 a plate.
equipment: large Dutch oven or heavy 6-quart pot with lid
notes: Thighs stay juicy through the long simmer; breast works, but add it with the potatoes for only the last 15 minutes and pull it as soon as it reaches 165°F. A packet of sazón with annatto can replace the cumin, turmeric, and garlic powder; read the label, since some blends contain wheat-based fillers. A handful of sliced pimiento-stuffed olives added with the potatoes is a common and welcome extra. If you use regular broth instead of gluten-free broth, check it for wheat. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days; the stew tastes even better on day two. Freeze it without the potatoes for up to 3 months, since potatoes turn grainy in the freezer. Reheat covered on the stove or in the microwave until it reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, trimmed and cut into 2-inch pieces
yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
carrots, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch rounds
cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: In a medium bowl, toss the chicken with 1 teaspoon of the salt, the oregano, cumin, turmeric, garlic powder, and lime juice. Let it sit while you chop the vegetables, 10 to 15 minutes, or cover and refrigerate for up to 8 hours.

Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the chicken in a single layer, in two batches if needed, and brown on one side without moving it, about 4 minutes. It does not need to cook through. Transfer to a plate, leaving the fat in the pot.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion, bell pepper, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and cook, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, until soft, 5 to 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic and half the cilantro and cook 1 minute, until fragrant. Add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute more, until it darkens slightly.
Pour in the tomato sauce and broth, then add the potatoes, carrots, bay leaf, and capers if using. Return the chicken and any juices on the plate to the pot and bring to a boil.

Cover, reduce the heat to medium-low, and simmer until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a knife and the chicken reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer, 25 to 30 minutes. Stir once or twice so nothing sticks to the bottom.

Uncover and simmer 5 to 10 minutes more, until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon. Remove the bay leaf, taste, and season with pepper and more salt if needed. Scatter the remaining cilantro over the top and serve over rice.

title: Dominican-Style Habichuelas Guisadas (Stewed Pinto Beans with Squash)
description: Pinto beans simmered with sofrito, tomato paste, oregano, and cubes of squash that melt into a thick, savory sauce. Spooned over rice, it makes six filling plates for about $1 each.
notes: The squash is what makes the sauce: it softens and falls apart, so mash a few pieces against the side of the pot if the beans look thin. Calabaza or kabocha are the closest to the Dominican auyama, and red kidney beans work in place of pinto. To start from dried beans, soak 1 1/2 cups (280 g) dried pinto beans overnight, simmer in fresh water until creamy, about 1 hour, and use 3 1/2 cups of beans plus 1 cup of their cooking liquid in place of the cans. Many cooks add a ham hock or a spoon of chicken bouillon; either makes the dish no longer vegan. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat with a splash of water until it reaches 165°F, since the beans thicken as they sit.

ingredients.name: butternut squash, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch cubes (about 10 oz)
pinto beans (15 oz each), not drained
cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: Heat the oil in a large heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and both bell peppers and cook, stirring often, until soft and starting to turn golden, 6 to 7 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and half the cilantro and cook 1 minute, until fragrant. Add the tomato paste and oregano and cook, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens to a brick red, about 2 minutes.
Add the squash, the beans with their liquid, the broth, and the salt. Stir well, scraping the bottom of the pot, and bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, until the squash is completely soft and starting to fall apart, 20 to 25 minutes.

Mash some of the squash and about a cup of the beans against the side of the pot and stir them in; the liquid should turn thick and creamy. If it is too thick, add a few tablespoons of water. Simmer 2 minutes more.
Taste and season with pepper and more salt if needed. Stir in the remaining cilantro and serve over rice.

title: Cuban-Style Ropa Vieja with Flank Steak, Peppers and Onions
description: Flank steak braised low and slow with peppers, onion, cumin, and tomato until it pulls apart into tender shreds. A pound and a half feeds six over rice, about $4 a plate.
equipment: large Dutch oven or heavy 6-quart pot with lid
notes: Flank steak gives the long strands the dish is named for; boneless chuck roast also works and costs less, though it shreds into shorter pieces and may need an extra 30 minutes. The beef is done when a fork twists through it with no resistance, so go by texture, not the clock. Replace the wine with more broth if you prefer; it only adds brightness. Sliced green olives stirred in with the capers are traditional if you have them. For a slow cooker, do the browning on the stove, then cook everything on low for 8 hours. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days, or freeze with plenty of sauce for up to 3 months. Reheat covered until steaming hot throughout, 165°F, and serve with black beans and rice.

ingredients.name: flank steak, cut crosswise into 3 pieces
large yellow onion, halved and thinly sliced
chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, for serving
cooked brown or white rice, for serving

instructions: Pat the steak dry and season all over with 1 teaspoon of the salt and the pepper. Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Brown the steak pieces until deeply browned, about 4 minutes per side, then transfer to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium and add the remaining tablespoon of oil, the onion, both bell peppers, and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook, stirring and scraping up the browned bits, until the vegetables are soft and lightly golden, 8 to 10 minutes.

Stir in the garlic, cumin, and oregano and cook 1 minute, until fragrant. Add the tomato paste and cook, stirring, for 1 minute. Pour in the wine, if using, and let it bubble until nearly gone, about 1 minute.
Add the tomato sauce, broth, and bay leaf and stir. Nestle the steak and its juices into the sauce so the meat is mostly covered, and bring to a boil.

Cover, reduce the heat to low, and simmer gently, turning the meat once halfway, until it pulls apart easily with a fork, 2 to 2 1/2 hours. The liquid should barely bubble; add a splash of water if it gets too low.

Lift the steak onto a cutting board and shred it along the grain into long strands with two forks. Meanwhile, simmer the sauce uncovered over medium heat until thick enough to cling to the vegetables, about 10 minutes.

Remove the bay leaf. Return the shredded beef to the pot along with the capers and vinegar, stir, and simmer 5 minutes so the meat soaks up the sauce. Taste for salt, sprinkle with parsley, and serve over rice.

title: Trinidad-Style Curry Channa and Aloo with Rice
description: Chickpeas and potato simmered in a Trinidad-style curry that is toasted in the pot first, served over plain rice instead of roti. Six hearty bowls from two cans of chickpeas, about $1.25 each.
notes: Cooking the curry paste in oil until it darkens, which Trinidadian cooks call burning the curry, removes the raw, dusty taste of the powder, so do not rush that step. Culantro, sold as shado beni, is traditional; cilantro is a good stand-in. Scotch bonnet is very hot: wear gloves to mince it, or drop it in whole and remove it before serving for gentle heat. To use dried chickpeas, soak 1 1/2 cups (300 g) overnight and simmer until tender, about 1 hour. Roti is the usual partner; rice keeps the meal gluten-free and cheaper. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 5 days; freeze up to 3 months, though the potato softens. Reheat with a splash of water until it reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: long grain white rice (280 g), rinsed
scotch bonnet or habanero chile, seeded and minced
chickpeas (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
large yukon gold potato (about 8 oz), peeled and cut into 3/4-inch cubes

instructions: Combine the rinsed rice, 2 1/4 cups water, and 1/4 teaspoon of the salt in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil. Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes while you make the curry.
In a small bowl, stir the curry powder and cumin with 1/4 cup water to make a smooth, loose paste.
Heat the oil in a large heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and chile and cook 1 minute, until fragrant.

Add the curry paste and cook, stirring constantly, until the water cooks off, the paste darkens a shade, and the oil starts to separate around the edges, 2 to 3 minutes. Lower the heat if it begins to stick hard.
Add the chickpeas and potato and stir for 2 minutes to coat them in the curry. Pour in 2 1/2 cups water, add the remaining 1 teaspoon salt and the thyme, and bring to a boil.

Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, partly covered and stirring occasionally, until the potato is tender and the sauce has thickened, about 25 minutes. Press some of the chickpeas and potato against the side of the pot to thicken the gravy further.
Remove the thyme stems. Stir in the garam masala and cilantro, season with pepper and more salt to taste, and serve over the fluffed rice.

title: Haitian-Style Diri ak Pwa (Rice and Red Beans with Thyme and Scallion)
description: Red kidney beans fried in the pot until their skins blister, then cooked with rice, thyme, scallion, and a whole hot pepper for aroma. A full pot that serves six costs about $4.
notes: Frying the beans until they blister and stick a little is what gives the rice its color and deep flavor, so let them catch before you add the vegetables. Keep the hot pepper whole and handle it gently; it perfumes the rice with little heat, but if it bursts the pot becomes very spicy. If you cook dried red kidney beans instead (1 cup, 190 g), boil them hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering until tender, because undercooked kidney beans can make people sick; save the cooking liquid to use in place of the canned liquid. Many Haitian cooks stir in a pat of butter at the end, which adds milk. Serve it as a side with stewed chicken, or as a meal with avocado and pikliz. Refrigerate rice within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days; reheat covered with a sprinkle of water until it reaches 165°F. It freezes well for up to 2 months.

ingredients.name: kidney beans (15 oz each), drained over a measuring cup to save the liquid
scallions, thinly sliced, whites and greens kept separate
long grain white rice (370 g), rinsed and drained
water, combined with the saved bean liquid
whole scotch bonnet or habanero chile, left intact

instructions: Heat the oil in a heavy 4-quart pot over medium-high heat. Add the drained beans and fry, stirring only every minute or so, until many of the skins split and blister and some beans stick and brown on the bottom, 5 to 6 minutes.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion, bell pepper, garlic, scallion whites, and parsley and cook, scraping up the browned bits, until the vegetables soften, about 4 minutes.
Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes so every grain is coated and lightly toasted. Pour in the water and bean liquid (3 1/4 cups total), add the salt, thyme, and whole chile, and bring to a boil.
Boil uncovered without stirring until the liquid drops just below the surface of the rice and small holes appear across the top, 5 to 7 minutes.
Cover tightly, turn the heat to low, and cook 20 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let the pot stand, still covered, for 10 minutes.

Carefully lift out the thyme stems and the chile without breaking it. Fluff the rice with a fork, season with pepper, and scatter the scallion greens over the top. Scrape up the crisp layer from the bottom of the pot and serve it alongside; it is a favorite part.

title: Vietnamese-Style Gà Kho Gừng (Caramelized Ginger Chicken)
description: Chicken thighs simmered in a dark homemade caramel with fish sauce, ginger, and black pepper until glossy and sticky. Salty-sweet and meant for lots of rice, it feeds four for about $8.
notes: Watch the caramel closely: pull it when it is the color of strong tea; pale caramel tastes only sweet, and if it smokes and smells burnt, start over, because the bitterness carries into the sauce. The caramel will sputter and may seize when the shallots and chicken go in; keep stirring and it melts back. Coconut water in place of the 1/2 cup water is a traditional, slightly sweeter variation. Most fish sauce is gluten-free, but some brands add wheat, so check the label. The sauce is intentionally salty, so serve it with plenty of rice and something fresh like sliced cucumber. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat covered until the chicken reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: boneless skinless chicken thighs, trimmed and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
fresh ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks (about a 2-inch piece)
serrano or green chile, thinly sliced
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: In a medium bowl, toss the chicken with the fish sauce and half the pepper. Let it sit 15 minutes while you prepare the aromatics.

Put the sugar and 2 tablespoons water in a 12-inch skillet over medium heat. Cook without stirring, swirling the pan now and then, until the sugar dissolves, bubbles, and turns a deep amber, 5 to 7 minutes. Watch it closely in the last minute, as it darkens fast.
As soon as the caramel is amber, carefully add the oil, shallots, garlic, and ginger; it will sputter. Stir for about 1 minute, until the shallots soften.

Add the chicken with all of its marinade and stir to coat. If the caramel hardens into lumps, keep stirring; it melts again as the chicken releases its juices. Add the 1/2 cup water and the salt and bring to a boil.

Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer uncovered, stirring every few minutes, until the sauce reduces to a dark, sticky glaze and the chicken reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer, 20 to 25 minutes. If the glaze gets too thick before the chicken is done, add a splash of water.
Stir in the remaining pepper, the scallions, and the chile if using, and cook 1 minute. Serve right away with the rice and sliced cucumber.

title: Filipino-Style Chicken Tinola with Ginger, Zucchini and Spinach
description: A clear, gingery chicken soup simmered from bone-in thighs and finished with zucchini and spinach. Water and bones make the broth, so six bowls with rice cost about $1.75 each.
notes: Green papaya or chayote is traditional; zucchini cooks much faster, so it goes in only at the end and should still hold its shape. Malunggay or chile pepper leaves are the usual greens, and spinach is the easy substitute. Boneless thighs work too; simmer them 15 to 20 minutes, until they reach 165°F, though the broth will be lighter. Most fish sauce is gluten-free, but some brands add wheat, so check the label. For young children, pull the meat off the bones before serving. Refrigerate within 2 hours and keep up to 4 days; freeze the broth and chicken without the vegetables for up to 3 months. Reheat until the soup comes to a boil or reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (about 6), skin removed
fresh ginger (3 inches), peeled and sliced into thin coins
serrano or green chile, left whole
medium zucchini, halved lengthwise and cut into 1-inch chunks
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: Heat the oil in a 6-quart pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the garlic and ginger and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Add the chicken and 2 tablespoons of the fish sauce. Cook, turning the pieces, until the outsides turn opaque and the chicken releases some juices, about 5 minutes.
Pour in the water, add the salt and the whole chile if using, and bring to a boil over high heat. Skim off any gray foam that rises to the surface.
Reduce the heat to medium-low, partly cover, and simmer gently until the meat is tender and a thermometer inserted next to the bone reads 165°F, about 30 minutes.
Add the zucchini and simmer until just tender but still holding its shape, 5 to 7 minutes. Turn off the heat, stir in the spinach, and let it wilt for 1 minute.
Taste the broth and add the remaining tablespoon of fish sauce and pepper as needed. Ladle into bowls with a thigh in each and serve with rice, with extra fish sauce at the table.

title: Thai-Style Stir-Fried Cabbage with Garlic and Fish Sauce
description: Half a cabbage seared hard in a hot pan with plenty of garlic, then tossed with fish sauce and a pinch of sugar. Charred edges, crisp ribs, and about 50 cents a serving.
notes: High heat and a pan that is not crowded are the whole trick; if your skillet is smaller than 12 inches, cook the cabbage in two batches or it will steam and go limp. Savoy or napa cabbage work too, and napa needs only 2 to 3 minutes. For a vegetarian version, replace the fish sauce with 1 1/2 tablespoons soy sauce, which swaps the fish allergen for wheat and soy; use gluten-free tamari to keep it gluten-free. Top with a fried egg or toss in leftover cooked chicken to make it a meal. Leftovers keep up to 3 days in the refrigerator, though the cabbage softens; refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat in a hot skillet until steaming. It does not freeze well.

ingredients.name: medium head green cabbage (about 1 1/2 lb), cored and cut into 2-inch pieces

instructions: Separate the cabbage pieces into individual layers so they cook evenly. In a small bowl, stir together the fish sauce, sugar, and water until the sugar dissolves.
Heat a wok or 12-inch skillet over high heat until a drop of water evaporates on contact. Add the oil and garlic and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, just until the garlic turns pale golden at the edges.

Add the cabbage and red pepper flakes and spread them out. Let the cabbage sit for 1 minute to char, then toss and let it sit again. Repeat for 4 to 5 minutes, until the edges are browned, the leaves have wilted, and the thick ribs are crisp-tender.

Pour the sauce around the edge of the pan so it sizzles, then toss for 30 seconds to coat. Taste, add a pinch of salt only if needed, season with pepper, and serve right away, ideally with jasmine rice.

title: Malaysian-Inspired Coconut Rice with Ginger and Lemongrass (Peanut-Free)
description: Jasmine rice cooked in coconut milk with lemongrass, ginger, and shallot, inspired by the rice in nasi lemak but made without peanuts or anchovies. Fragrant enough to anchor a meal at about 60 cents a serving.
notes: Pandan leaf is the traditional flavoring; if you find it, tie two leaves in a knot and add them with the lemongrass. Nasi lemak is classically served with fried peanuts, crisp anchovies, sambal, and egg, so this version keeps the rice safe for families avoiding peanuts and fish; add a hard-boiled egg (adds eggs) or fried tofu (adds soy) to make it a meal. Coconut is not one of the major US food allergens, but anyone with a tree-nut allergy should check with their doctor. A thin golden layer on the bottom is normal; a burnt smell means the heat was too high. Rice should be refrigerated within 2 hours (sooner is better) and keeps up to 4 days; reheat covered with a sprinkle of water until steaming, 165°F. It freezes well in portions for up to 2 months.

ingredients.name: full-fat coconut milk (13.5 oz), well stirred
lemongrass stalk, trimmed, tough outer layer removed, bruised and tied in a knot
fresh ginger (1 inch), peeled and thinly sliced
english cucumber, thinly sliced, for serving

instructions: Rinse the rice in a bowl of cold water, swishing with your hand and pouring off the cloudy water, 3 or 4 times until the water is mostly clear. Drain well in a strainer for 5 minutes.
In a heavy 3-quart saucepan, whisk the coconut milk, water, salt, and sugar until smooth. Add the rice, lemongrass, ginger, and shallot and stir to combine.
Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring gently along the bottom every minute so the coconut milk does not scorch, 5 to 6 minutes.
Cover tightly, turn the heat to the lowest setting, and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes.
While the rice rests, toast the coconut flakes in a dry small skillet over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until golden, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer to a plate right away so they do not burn.
Remove the lemongrass and ginger, fluff the rice with a fork, and serve topped with the toasted coconut and sliced cucumber on the side.

title: Indonesian-Style Nasi Goreng with Fried Eggs and Cabbage
description: Leftover rice stir-fried with shallots, garlic, chile, and a sweet soy glaze, then topped with a crisp-edged fried egg. A fridge clean-out that feeds four for about $1.50 a plate.
notes: Cold, day-old rice fries into separate grains; freshly cooked rice turns mushy, so if that is all you have, spread it on a sheet pan and refrigerate it uncovered for 30 minutes first. If you have kecap manis, the Indonesian sweet soy sauce, use 3 tablespoons in place of the dark soy sauce and brown sugar. For gluten-free, use gluten-free tamari for both soy sauces and check the ketchup label. Shrimp paste (terasi) is traditional and adds shellfish; leftover chicken cooked to 165°F is a good addition but makes it no longer vegetarian. Runny yolks are not recommended for young children, pregnant people, or older adults; cook the eggs until the yolks are firm for them. Refrigerate leftover rice within 2 hours, keep up to 3 days without the eggs, and reheat in a skillet until it reaches 165°F.

ingredients.name: cold cooked jasmine rice (from about 1 2/3 cups raw, 310 g)
lime, cut into wedges, for serving

instructions: In a small bowl, stir together the dark soy sauce, soy sauce, brown sugar, and ketchup until the sugar dissolves. Break up any clumps in the rice with damp fingers so the grains separate.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a wok or 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Add the shallots and cook, stirring, until golden at the edges, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the garlic and chile and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the cabbage and carrot and stir-fry until the cabbage wilts, about 2 minutes.
Raise the heat to high. Add the rice and salt and toss, pressing the rice against the hot pan, until it is heated through and a few grains turn crisp, 3 to 4 minutes.
Pour the sauce over the rice and toss for 1 to 2 minutes, until every grain is evenly brown and glossy and a little sauce caramelizes on the pan. Stir in the scallions and divide among 4 plates.

Heat the remaining tablespoon of oil in a 10-inch nonstick skillet over medium heat. Crack in the eggs and fry until the whites are set and the edges are lacy and crisp, 2 to 3 minutes, or longer for firm yolks.
Top each plate with a fried egg and serve with cucumber, cherry tomatoes, and lime wedges on the side.
